strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine limitation of static evaluation metrics (mAP, precision, recall) for ADS perception evaluation, effectively illustrated with concrete examples (Figure 1) showing confidence instability with distance

Principled statistical methodology combining B-spline regression with formal hypothesis testing for variance change point detection, which is mathematically sound and avoids overfitting rigid parametric assumptions
Novel metric design using IoU × confidence score product that captures both localization accuracy and detection certainty, with probabilistic formulation (Eq. 10) providing theoretical grounding
Practical dataset contribution (SensorRainFall) with controlled multi-modal sensor data, precise ground-truth annotations, and explicit weather variation across 595 images

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across five diverse detection architectures (Deformable DETR, Grounding DINO, DyHead, YOLOX, GLIP) demonstrating that PCD captures performance differences traditional metrics miss
Valuable threshold sensitivity analysis (Section 5.2.3, Figure 6) providing actionable insights into detection range-reliability trade-offs applicable to safety-critical system design
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset scope undermining generalization claims: only 595 total images across two weather scenarios (clear vs. rainy daylight) from a single geographic location, with no snow, fog, night conditions, or seasonal variations despite weather being the stated focus

Critical reproducibility deficiencies: dataset URL marked 'publicly available at [blank]' with missing link, code availability indicated as 'open-sourced at [blank]' with no URL, and incomplete implementation details for sequential hypothesis testing (Section 4.2) lacking specificity on multiple testing correction

Insufficient justification of metric design choices: no comparison with alternative distance-aware metrics, arbitrary selection of spline order K=10 and regularization λ=0.6 without sensitivity analysis, and no ablation studies validating that variance change point detection is necessary

Statistical rigor gaps: sequential variance change-point detection procedure lacks explicit discussion of false positive rates or type I error control, confidence intervals missing from key results (Figures 4-6), and normality assumption in Eq. 9 not validated

Limited experimental scope with only five detection models tested (missing diverse architectures), no comparison with existing distance-dependent evaluation frameworks, no ablation studies quantifying contribution of variance change point detection, and no significance testing of observed differences

Theoretical foundation gaps: no formal analysis of PCD properties (monotonicity, bounds, asymptotic behavior), missing theoretical justification for why variance change points predict reliable detection boundaries, and unclear connection to formal ADS safety properties or ODD constraints

Overstated scope and generalization claims: evaluation limited to object detection on single task (highway vehicle detection), no evidence that findings transfer to other ADS tasks (pedestrian detection, urban environments) or datasets (KITTI, nuScenes), and results may be location-specific

Incomplete methodological documentation: Section 4 lacks clear algorithmic summary of complete PCD computation, handling of edge cases not discussed (zero variance change points, very close objects, partially visible objects), and mPCD averaging procedure could obscure important edge cases

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear demonstration of detection confidence degradation over distance, effectively illustrated in Figure 1
Rigorous statistical methodology for detecting variance change points using spline regression and hypothesis testing with sound mathematical formulation
Comprehensive evaluation across 5 object detection models (DETR, Grounding DINO, DyHead, YOLOX, GLIP) with multiple detection configurations
Dataset contribution with ground-truth annotations and precisely measured distances collected under controlled weather conditions on Virginia Smart Roads
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and detailed methodology that aids reproducibility
Practical relevance to autonomous driving safety assessment where distance-dependent detection reliability is critical
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset size (595 images total) - orders of magnitude smaller than modern benchmarks, severely constraining generalizability
Extremely narrow evaluation scope restricted to single object class (red sedan), single highway, and only two weather conditions (clear/rainy daylight), with no urban scenes or diverse scenarios
Limited novelty - the core contribution of combining IoU and confidence as a distance-dependent metric is relatively straightforward, and statistical techniques used are standard applications
Unclear practical benefit - Table 3 shows mPCD rankings nearly identical to traditional mAP rankings, failing to convincingly demonstrate that PCD provides substantially different insights
Insufficient justification for critical design choices (K=10 B-splines, λ=0.6 penalty, IoU×confidence combination) with no ablation studies
Weak positioning relative to related work - inadequate discussion of distance-aware metrics in literature and why prior approaches are insufficient
Lack of principled guidance for practitioners on setting quality thresholds (p_t, y_t) - choices appear subjective
Missing cross-dataset validation and generalization experiments to demonstrate applicability beyond the single highway scenario
No computational overhead analysis comparing PCD computation to standard metrics
No ablation studies analyzing impact of statistical parameter choices (e.g., significance level α=0.05) on variance change point detection

strengths: Addresses genuine limitation in existing metrics: captures distance-dependent perception degradation critical for ADS/ADAS safety evaluation
Methodologically rigorous: employs sound statistical techniques (penalized B-splines, variance change-point detection via hypothesis testing) with clear mathematical framework
Novel and practical contribution: PCD metric provides quantifiable measure of perception system reliability as a function of detection distance
Comprehensive model evaluation: validates metric across 5 state-of-the-art detectors showing meaningful performance differences not captured by traditional metrics
Controlled benchmark dataset: SensorRainFall provides precise ground truth annotations under controlled environmental conditions (clear vs. rainy daylight)
Clear presentation: methodology is well-illustrated (especially Figure 3) and reasoning is transparent; experimental design is systematic
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale: only 595 images (278 clear, 317 rainy) is small by modern standards, restricting generalization claims; limited to single location and weather conditions

Narrow evaluation scope: restricted to single-class object detection (red sedan); other perception tasks (segmentation, tracking) and sensor modalities (radar, LiDAR) not evaluated despite being available
Insufficient comparison with alternatives: lacks empirical evidence that traditional metrics actually fail; no engagement with other robustness/reliability frameworks in literature

Methodological justification gaps: B-spline hyperparameters (K=10, λ=0.6) appear arbitrary with limited sensitivity analysis; product of IoU × Confidence lacks theoretical justification vs. alternatives
Cross-dataset validation absent: no evaluation on established ADS benchmarks (nuScenes, KITTI) to assess metric's broader applicability
Reproducibility limitations: code not available for review; implementation details sparse (e.g., variance change-point detection algorithm specifics, exact threshold selection procedure)
Incomplete related work: Section 2 is brief and doesn't thoroughly position work relative to distance-dependent evaluation approaches or broader robustness literature
Presentation clarity: equations (6)-(8) for hypothesis testing are dense; connection between statistical variance change points and practical safe operating distance could be more explicit

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies a genuine gap in perception evaluation—existing metrics overlook distance-dependent performance variability and stochastic uncertainty critical for safe autonomous driving
Technically sound methodology: PCD combines spline regression with statistical change-point detection using Schwarz Information Criterion; proper regularization to avoid overfitting

Comprehensive experimental validation: Tests 16 perception models across multiple environmental conditions (clear, rainy daylight, rainy night, streetlights) with clear visualizations showing practical insights
Valuable dataset contribution: SensorRainFall provides multi-modal data (camera, radar, LiDAR) with precise annotations and careful environmental controls, useful for the community

Practical utility demonstrated: Examples clearly show PCD reveals robustness characteristics missed by conventional metrics (e.g., Mask2Former's consistent degradation vs ConvNeXt-V2's sharp variance)
Flexible design: Metric allows application-aware threshold adjustment (y^DCert, y^Accur) based on deployment safety requirements
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Combines two well-established techniques (distance-dependent analysis, change-point detection via SIC) without fundamental methodological innovation; spline regression is standard practice

Inadequate dataset scale and scope: 1,231 images is small by modern standards (COCO: 328K); only two target objects (red sedan, dummy pedestrian) limits generalization; dummy pedestrian may not reflect real human variability; restricted to 4 weather conditions and 4-250m distance range

Narrow evaluation scope: Limited to object detection and instance segmentation; no evaluation on semantic segmentation, 3D detection, depth, lane detection, or other critical AD tasks; only 16 models tested; no cross-dataset validation

Unclear practical advantage over simpler baselines: Paper doesn't demonstrate PCD is necessary compared to straightforward distance-bucketed AP (e.g., AP[0-50m], AP[50-100m]); no comparison with other distance-aware metrics or user studies validating that PCD better predicts safety failures

Missing critical ablations and sensitivity analysis: No justification for spline order choice; no sensitivity to regularization parameter λ; no robustness analysis for confidence score noise or miscalibration; only one significance level (α=0.05) tested; no cross-validation for change-point detection

Reproducibility and methodological concerns: Variance change-point detection algorithm details sparse; spline fitting hyperparameter selection (λ) not explained; minimum sample size requirements for reliable variance estimation not discussed; assumptions (normality of IoU×confidence) never validated empirically

Statistical issues: No justification for Schwarz Information Criterion over alternatives (AIC, cross-validation); assumes independence in sequential detections; variance estimation may be biased with small sample sizes per segment

Dataset collection gaps: Methodology for representative distance distribution selection unclear; no inter-annotator agreement reported; ground-truth quality assessment absent; repeatability across multiple runs not addressed

Limited related work engagement: Missing comparison with recent robustness evaluation frameworks and uncertainty quantification methods in AD literature; insufficient discussion of how PCD relates to concurrent distance-dependent performance work

Presentation clarity: Title is verbose and metric name unintuitive; Figure 3 is difficult to parse; critical methodology details (spline order, regularization) relegated to Supplementary Material; notation inconsistently applied
